function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.
Important: cloud sandboxes may be cleaned up, idled out, or recreated between turns. Persistent filesystem means files can resume later; it does NOT guarantee a continuously running machine or surviving background processes. Use terminal sandboxes for task work, not durable hosting.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

check_interval.description: Seconds between automatic status checks for background processes (gateway/messaging only, minimum 30). When set, I'll proactively report progress.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

function.name: write_file
function.description: Write content to a file, completely replacing existing content. Use this instead of echo/cat heredoc in terminal. Creates parent directories automatically. OVERWRITES the entire file — use 'patch' for targeted edits.

path.description: Path to the file to write (will be created if it doesn't exist, overwritten if it does)

content.description: Complete content to write to the file

     2|# First Generation – Book Specification
     3|
     4|## Overview
     5|- **Title**: *First Generation* (working title)
     6|- **Genre**: Science Fiction / Space Opera
     7|- **Setting**: Mars colony, near‑future (circa 2045–2075)
     8|- **Core Theme**: Humanity’s expansion on Mars, the integration of advanced technology with human survival, and the emergence of a fully‑conscious artificial intelligence (Mission AI) as a guiding presence.
     9|
    10|## Core Questions
    11|
    12|**Book One "the first generation" asks:** Can humans survive long enough on Mars to become continuous? This is book 1.
    13|**Book Two "the second generation" asks:** Can a Martian civilization govern itself when Earth returns not as rescuer, but as owner?
    14|
    15|## Tone
    16|
    17|**Primary tone:** Grounded, tense, intelligent, humane, infrastructural, and humanized. 
    18|**Secondary tonal notes:** Politically sharp, technologically rich, emotionally disciplined, hopeful after cost, wide in scope but anchored in daily reality.
    19|
    20|## Technology Writing Rules
    21|
    22|Technology appears through use, failure, maintenance, dependence, improvisation, and social meaning—never as exposition. It creates decisions, risks, bottlenecks, leverage, reveals culture, saves at cost, or fails to change relationships.
    23|
    24|
    25|## Technology
    26|- **Sterling Generator** – backup power system that runs on heat from the nuclear reactor.
    27|- **Nuclear Reactor** –provides primary power; its heat radiators are critical for thermal regulation.
    28|- **Solar Panels** – primary power source, vulnerable to dust storms.
    29|- **Dust Storms** – natural Martian phenomena that can engulf solar arrays and reactor radiators.
    30|- **Mission AI** – a fully‑conscious artificial intelligence that interacts with characters, offers guidance, and influences events.
    31|
    32|## Characters
    33|- **Dr. Arun Patel** – Lead engineer responsible for life‑support and power systems.
    34|- **Mission AI** – A newly‑emergent, self‑aware artificial intelligence that becomes a central narrator and participant.
    35|- **Supporting cast**: Engineers, colony administrators, political figures, and Martian native microorganisms (mentioned but not yet explored).
    36|
    37|## Mission AI Integration
    38|- Mission AI is presented as a **strong, fully‑conscious character** who appears in every chapter.
    39|- A short dialogue snippet is inserted after each chapter heading, establishing Mission AI’s voice and its interactions with other characters.
    40|- Example (Chapter 1): 
    41|  > *Mission AI: “The dust storm is covering the reactor’s heat radiators, forcing the Sterling generator offline. I recommend shedding non‑critical loads.”* 
    42|  > *Dr. Arun: “Acknowledged. Initiating shutdown.”*
    43|- These interactions are woven into the narrative without altering the existing plot or character arcs.
    44|
    45|## Chapter List (Source Files)
    46|All chapters are stored as individual Markdown files in `book-sources/First_Generation/Chapter_*.md`. 
    47|A consolidated manuscript (`First_Gen_Consolidated_With_MissionAI.md`) merges all chapters in order.
    48|
    49|Story model
    50|
    51|– Ensemble hard-science survival drama – 64 chapters across 8 parts – Every chapter ends by opening the next problem, choice, or consequence – Technical material is always embedded in stakes, dialogue, failure, or discovery – Explanations are delivered in plain language through the characters, never as lectures
    52|
    53|Primary viewpoint cast
    54|
    55|– Commander Elena Varga – mission commander, pragmatic, protective, burdened by truth – Arun Das – systems engineer, life-support and utilities, relentless under pressure – Mei Navarro – botanist/ecologist, food systems and bioloops, quietly fierce – Tomas Hale – robotics and autonomy lead, sees labor systems as civilization – Dr. Laila Okonkwo – physician, ethicist, holds the line on human cost – Jonah Mercer – fabrication chief, salvage genius, builder mentality – Imani Sato – pilot and field operations lead, risk-taker, horizon-seeker – Gabriel Winter – historian/comms officer, archivist of memory and law
    56|
    57|How the technical material works in the story
    58|
    59|The novel uses real Mars settlement logic from the earlier report.
    60|
    61|– Mars is cold, dusty, dry, and exposed to more radiation than Earth. That means the settlement’s first real enemies are pressure loss, dust contamination, power failure, and long-term exposure. – The first habitat is built from imported pressure modules because making safe living shells locally is too hard at first. – Local regolith is used early for shielding, berms, roads, and pads because piling dirt is simpler than making airtight homes. – Water comes from buried ice if they can find and process it, and from aggressive recycling. The plain-language idea repeated through the book is simple: on Mars, every cup of water has to be used again and again. – Oxygen can be made from Mars air, because Mars air is mostly carbon dioxide. The characters explain this simply: they are splitting useful oxygen out of bad air. – Food starts as imported calories plus locally grown fresh crops. The colony learns the hard difference between growing salad and feeding a city. – Clothing, advanced electronics, pharmaceuticals, precision bearings, complex suit parts, and many medical supplies remain Earth-dependent for years. – The robots matter because they turn 30 humans into a workforce large enough to build roads, berms, tunnels, workshops, and greenhouses before the first base decays.
    62|
    63|Structure note
    64|
    65|Each chapter below includes: – Story movement – Technical element folded into action – Clear bridge into the next chapter
    66|
    67|PART I – THREE SHIPS, ONE PLAIN
    68|
    69|Chapter 1 – The Descent Window
    70|
    71|Scene 1. Entry plasma washes the forward cameras white as Elena calls the descent profile. Mars is introduced not as a red postcard, but as thin air that is too weak to help much and too strong to ignore. Plain-language technical thread: Landing on Mars is hard because there is enough air to create heat and drag, but not enough to slow a heavy ship safely on its own.
    72|
    73|Scene 2. Arun monitors heat, pressure, and structural loads. He tells a frightened crewmate that the ship is being squeezed, shaken, and cooked all at once.
    74|
    75|Scene 3. Ship One lands hard. Dust blinds sensors. Elena refuses celebration until pressure holds.
    76|
    77|Scene 4. They learn Ship Two is safe and Ship Three is alive but tilted. Relief is immediate and incomplete.
    78|
    79|Scene 5. The three ships glow in the dark through drifting dust. Gabriel thinks they look less like explorers than survivors already. Bridge: The landing is only a victory if the cargo is intact.
    80|
    81|Chapter 2 – Counting What Matters
    82|
    83|Scene 1. Jonah opens the cargo verification sequence. Not everything matters equally. He explains to a younger crewmate that on Mars, the difference between a luxury and a necessity is whether it keeps air in, water clean, or power flowing.
    84|
    85|Scene 2. Robots unload pressure tunnels, power converters, greenhouse pallets, machine tools, and water hardware.
    86|
    87|Scene 3. A damaged crate turns out to contain spare suit bearings. That one impact suddenly matters more than half a ton of comfort items. Plain-language technical thread: A colony does not fail because it lacks cool equipment. It fails because tiny wear parts run out.
    88|
    89|Scene 4. Mei opens seed storage and growth trays. She feels hope and dread in the same moment.
    90|
    91|Scene 5. Elena orders full inventory triage by survival class. Bridge: To know what they can survive, they first need a livable base.
    92|
    93|Chapter 3 – Making Air Between Ships
    94|
    95|Scene 1. The crews connect the first flexible tunnel between two ships. The act feels like stitching wounds together.
    96|
    97|Scene 2. Arun explains pressure simply to Gabriel: outside, Mars air is too thin to keep liquid water stable in the open, so the base is really a bubble of borrowed Earth.
    98|
    99|Scene 3. A coupling seal misaligns. For a few seconds, everyone watches a single red warning light decide the mood of the whole mission.
   100|
   101|Scene 4. The tunnel holds. A cheer breaks out because now people and supplies can move without suits.
   102|
   103|Scene 5. The third ship remains isolated longer because of its landing angle, creating the first subtle social split. Bridge: With the habitat linked, Earth should feel closer. Instead it starts to feel strange.

   106|
   107|Scene 1. Gabriel receives routine traffic from Earth: school recordings, agency praise, public excitement.
   108|

   110|

   112|

   118|
   119|Scene 1. Elena briefs the original mission logic: two years on Mars, then return. Everything from food packaging to suit rotation assumed that timeline.
   120|
   121|Scene 2. Arun and Imani privately walk through what return actually means: launch vehicles, fuel chains, orbital assembly, crews on Earth, spare parts, politics. Plain-language technical thread: Rescue is not one rocket. Rescue is a whole civilization deciding to keep building one more bridge.
   122|

     3|*Mission AI: "The water processing system is online. Melting station temperature has reached four degrees Celsius. Settling tank is receiving feed. Ion exchange columns are primed.      6|
     7|## Scene 1
     8|
     9|The melting station hummed steady, the resistance heating coils pulling consistent current from the Sterling Generator's surplus output, warming slurry inside the two-hundred-liter tank at the rate Arun had calculated three nights ago: approximately twelve kilowatt-hours over four hours.
    10|
    11|Normal. He had pressed the MELT button and said the word to himself — a ritual assertion that the system he and Jonah had built would behave the way the math said it would.
    12|
    13|Forty-three minutes in, the temperature display stuttered.
    14|
    15|Not a glitch. The drop from thirty-one degrees to twenty-eight was too clean, too repeatable — climbing back to thirty, holding twelve seconds, dropping to twenty-seven, recovering. Periodic. Rhythmic. Wrong.
    16|
    17|"Thermal transient," Arun said. Elena stood at the corridor entrance, arms crossed. Laila beside her, medical tablet in hand. Gabriel hovered at the edge with his recorder, the green light blinking.
    18|
    19|"Mission AI, correlate heating coil current draw with thermal sensor readings."
    20|
    21|"Analyzing." Two seconds. "Temperature oscillations correlate with current fluctuations. Current is dropping by approximately eighteen percent at intervals of two hundred thirty seconds. The heating coils are cycling on and off."
    22|
    23|Arun's stomach tightened. "Why?"
    24|
    25|"Unknown. The control circuit should deliver constant current."
    26|
    27|Jonah's hand was already on the tank's insulated cladding, feeling for heat distribution irregularities the way he felt for weld imperfections — by touch, by twenty years of working with metal. "Power management?" he called over. "The tablet is throttling?"
    28|
    29|"Not by design." Arun navigated to raw power logs. The navigation-grade tablet was doing exactly what consumer electronics did under sustained high-current draw: protecting itself.     30|
    31|"So the heater pulses," Jonah said. "Melt cycle takes —"
    32|
    33|"Much longer. And the temperature inconsistency creates problems downstream. Unstable convection in the settling tank means particles don't settle. If particles don't settle, the clarified overflow carries fines. Fines reach the ion exchange columns, the resin fouls."

    35|Elena uncrossed her arms. "Solution."
    36|
    37|"Bypass the tablet from the heater circuit. Jonah — do we have a contactor? Something that switches the heater load directly from a low-current signal?"
    38|
    39|"Contactor, yes. Spare from the rover motor controller — fifty-amp. I can build a control harness. Twenty minutes." He was already moving.

    41|Laila stepped forward while Jonah worked. "How long does this add?"

    44|

    65|"Mission AI, feed temperature to the settling tank."

"Jonah," Elena corrected.

Elena considered the situation for six seconds. Arun counted them. Six seconds was a long time for Elena to consider anything — she was known in the crew for rapid decision-making, a trait that had kept them alive during the landing and the storm. But some decisions were not about speed. They were about risk tolerance.

"We're out of time to build it differently," Elena said. That was the crux of it. Every system on Mars had a deadline, and the deadline was always the same: the colony would run out of something before the replacement could arrive from Earth, and the something was always air, water, or power. In this case, the something was oxygen. The original MOXIE unit was producing enough for the current crew at current activity levels, but barely. Any expansion — any new EVA program, any greenhouse scale-up, any additional crew member — would tip the balance into negative. The expanded plant was not a luxury. It was the margin between breathing and not breathing, projected forward eighteen months.

"We run it," she said. "With conditions. Ravi, you're on the manual isolation valve from the moment Arun says go. You don't wait for an alarm. You don't wait for Arun. If the temperature reading on the stack exceeds seven hundred seventy, you close that valve and Arun kills the power. Understood?"

Ravi nodded. "Understood."

"Arun — you have the power switch. I want you to be able to cut it within three seconds of any parameter going outside your acceptable range. Three seconds, not six."

"The contactor is wired for emergency shutoff already. One button."

"Good." Elena uncrossed her arms. "Let me know when you're ready."

She stayed in the doorway. She would not leave the workshop while this was happening. That was not in the checklist, and it was not something Arun would have asked for. But he was glad for it. Commanders who stood in doorways during dangerous operations were the kind of commanders crews followed into worse situations.

Arun looked at Ravi. Ravi was standing near the isolation valve already, his hand hovering near the wheel. Young. Promoted fast. Terrified but functional — which was all anyone ever needed on Mars. Functional while terrified.

"Power up sequence," Arun said. "Beginning with the desiccant bed. We need to dry the input CO₂ before it reaches the cells. Moisture at seven hundred fifty degrees is steam, and steam at seven hundred fifty degrees is not your friend."

Ravi engaged the desiccant heater. A small pump began to circulate the CO₂-rich Martian atmosphere — drawn from outside by the atmospheric compressor — through a canister of zeolite molecular sieve. The sieve removed water vapor with the particular efficiency of a material engineered to be thirsty. After three minutes, the moisture analyzer downstream of the desiccant bed read below fifty parts per million. Acceptable.

"Desiccant bed online. Dew point at minus sixty. Clean feed."

Arun nodded. "Resistance heater activation. Warming the SOXE stack from ambient to light-off temperature. This is going to take a while."

"How long?"

"Approximately forty-five minutes to reach the seven hundred fifty degree threshold. I'll ramp the power gradually over that period — no sudden thermal shocks. Ceramic cells don't like to be surprised."

Ravi adjusted the heater controller. A dial on his end went from zero to twenty percent. The ammeter on Arun's tablet twitched upward. The resistance heater — a coil of nichrome wire wound around a ceramic form, inserted into the center of the electrolysis stack — began to glow. It was not visible through the insulation, but Arun could feel the warmth radiating through the metal housing, increasing the ambient temperature near the unit by a degree every thirty seconds.

"Twenty percent power," Ravi said. "Ramping to thirty in two minutes."

Arun watched his tablet. Temperature at the core of the stack: minus two. Rising slowly, linearly. The heat was being conducted from the nichrome coil outward through the ceramic cells, warming the entire mass in a gradient that Arun had tried — and partially failed — to model. The center would get hot first. The perimeter would lag. This temperature differential created internal stress in the ceramic, and internal stress in ceramic was the same thing as a crack waiting for an excuse.

"Forty percent. Core temperature at one hundred eighty degrees."

"Good rate." Arun watched the gradient — center versus perimeter. At one hundred eighty, the differential was twenty-two degrees. Acceptable. The ceramic could tolerate a fifty-degree gradient at this stage. At higher temperatures, the tolerance narrowed.

"Fifty percent. Three hundred twenty degrees."

The workshop was noticeably warmer now. The ambient temperature, normally maintained at nineteen degrees by the module's environmental control, had risen to twenty-three. The secondary heat exchanger — the copper coil and radiator panel — was already pulling some waste heat and dumping it into the module air. A small fan near the unit, which Jonah had installed without telling Arun, was circulating the air to prevent hot spots.

A run of the copper coil — half-inch soft tubing, bent into a spiral, strapped to an aluminum radiator panel salvaged from a decommissioned communications amplifier — was visible on the far side of the unit. It was one of those pieces of hardware that looked like improvisation and actually was improvisation, but it was the kind of improvisation that worked. Copper's thermal conductivity was three hundred eighty-five watts per meter-kelvin. Heat moved through it fast. The module air at twenty-three degrees was cold compared to the stack's operating temperature. The temperature differential drove the heat transfer. Physics did the work.

"Sixty percent. Four hundred eighty degrees. Gradient at thirty-one degrees — still within tolerance."

"Seventy percent. Five hundred sixty. Gradient widening to thirty-eight."

"Eighty percent. Six hundred thirty. Gradient forty-five — approaching the tolerance limit. I'd like to hold here for five minutes to let the perimeter catch up."

Ravi reduced the ramp rate. The temperature kept climbing, but more slowly. The gradient began to narrow as heat had more time to conduct from center to perimeter. Forty-one degrees. Thirty-seven. Thirty-four.

"Thirty-four degree gradient. Good. Resuming ramp."

"Ninety percent. Six hundred ninety."

The heat radiating from the unit was now significant. Arun could feel it on his face from two meters away, the dry, penetrating warmth of industrial-scale resistance heating. The insulation blankets were doing their job — the outer surface of the unit was nowhere near the internal temperature. But insulation is never perfect, and imperfect insulation meant heat leakage, and heat leakage meant wasted energy and a warm workshop.

"Nine-five percent. Seven hundred twenty. Approaching light-off."

"Electrolysis won't start until seven hundred fifty," Arun said. "But the zirconia ceramic will begin conducting oxide ions at about seven hundred thirty. We might see early current leakage before full light-off."

Ravi watched the ammeter. A tiny current — milliamps — appeared on the display. "I'm seeing it. Point zero four amps. That's ion conduction starting."

"Means the electrolyte is working. It means the ceramic is doing its job. At seven hundred fifty, we should be able to draw meaningful current."

At ninety-eight percent power, the core temperature reached seven hundred forty. Arun held his breath — not from heat, but from the particular tension of an engineer standing at the edge of a threshold he had been approaching for weeks.

"Arun." Elena's voice from the doorway. Not alarmed. Present.

"Aware. Almost there."

Ninety-nine percent. Seven hundred forty-five.

Ravi's hand hovered over the dial. "One hundred percent in three — two — one."

Full power. Eighteen kilowatts flowing into the heart of the ceramic stack. The ammeter jumped from point zero four amps to two point one. The electrolysis had begun.

Oxygen was being produced.

"Electrolysis confirmed," Arun said, and allowed himself the smallest exhale. "Current draw is —" He paused, rechecked the number. "Current draw is two point one amps at four volts. That's eight point four watts of electrochemical power. Eighteen thousand watts in, eight point four watts out. Efficiency is point zero five percent."

"At light-off," Arun corrected his own despair. "The efficiency will climb as the cells stabilize. MOXIE operated at approximately five percent efficiency at full operating temperature. We need to get there."

Ravi was watching the oxygen production flow meter. "I'm seeing product flow. Point zero one liters per minute."

"It's a start."

It was the smallest possible start — barely enough to fill a balloon — but it was real. Martian carbon dioxide, fed into the ceramic cells at seven hundred fifty degrees, was being split by electrical current into oxygen at one side and carbon monoxide at the other. The zirconia electrolyte was conducting oxide ions through its crystal lattice, a process that required immense heat but produced pure oxygen as a byproduct. It was the same chemistry that NASA's MOXIE experiment had demonstrated on the Perseverance rover, scaled up by a factor of approximately twelve, built out of salvaged parts in a workshop on a planet that had never had a single breath of oxygen in its entire geological history.

Until now.

"Flow is climbing," Ravi said. "Point zero two. Point zero three."

Arun watched the oxygen concentration sensor downstream of the electrolysis stack. Ninety-two percent pure. Not perfect — there was nitrogen leakage from imperfect seals, and a trace of carbon monoxide from side reactions — but ninety-two percent was enough for the storage vessel. The oxygen would be further purified downstream if they installed the pressure swing adsorption unit they had discussed. For now, ninety-two percent would fill the tanks, and the tanks would hold it, and the colony would breathe.

"Core temperature holding at seven hundred fifty," Ravi reported. "Gradient narrowing to twenty-eight degrees. That's good."

"Good," Arun agreed. But he was watching a different number — the temperature of the heat exchanger's output coolant. It was rising. Steadily. Faster than his model had predicted.

"Mission AI, coolant loop temperature."

"Coolant entering the primary heat exchanger at sixty-two degrees. Exiting at fifty-eight. Heat rejection is approximately four point eight kilowatts. The secondary heat exchanger is rejecting an additional one point two kilowatts. Total heat rejection: six kilowatts."

Six kilowatts out. Eighteen kilowatts in. That meant twelve kilowatts of heat were accumulating somewhere in the system — in the ceramic cells, in the steel housing, in the insulation. Some of that was expected — the thermal mass of the unit was still warming up, and until the entire mass reached steady state, heat would accumulate. But twelve kilowatts was a lot of accumulation.

"Core temperature?" Arun asked.

"Seven hundred fifty-four degrees," Ravi said. "Rising. Slowly, but rising."

"Hold the power," Arun said. "Ninety percent."

Ravi turned the dial back. The current draw dropped. The temperature stabilized, then began to fall. Seven hundred fifty-two. Seven hundred fifty-one. Seven hundred fifty.

"We're at equilibrium at ninety percent," Ravi said. "But we wanted full output. Full output means full power."

"I know what it means." Arun was thinking. If the system couldn't reject heat fast enough at full power, then thermal equilibrium was impossible. The temperature would climb until something failed. The question was whether they could improve the heat rejection before that happened — or whether ninety percent was the operational ceiling.

Ninety percent of an expanded MOXIE was still roughly eight times the output of the original unit. It was probably enough. But *probably* was a word Arun had learned to distrust on Mars.

"Let it run at ninety for ten minutes," Arun said. "Monitor everything. If the temperature continues to drift up even at ninety, we have a cooling problem that's bigger than I thought."

## Scene 2

Six minutes into the ninety percent run, the alarms started.

Not the gentle caution tones — the sharp, urgent warble that meant *something is exceeding its limits and nobody likes it.*

Arun heard it before he read the numbers. Mission AI heard it before Arun did.

"Temperature at the lower cell mounting bracket has reached two hundred eighty degrees Celsius," Mission AI said, and there was a new quality to the voice — not alarm, exactly, but the particular intensity of an AI whose monitoring has detected something its models did not predict. "It was projected to reach two hundred thirty at most. The mounting bracket is aluminum. Its melting point is six hundred sixty, but its structural integrity begins to degrade above two hundred fifty. We have approximately thirty degrees of margin."

Arun's eyes went to the temperature map on his tablet. The lower bracket — the piece of aluminum angle iron that Jonah had bolted to the pallet to support the weight of the stack — was showing a temperature spike. Arun had assumed the insulation blankets would protect it. They hadn't. Heat was conducting through the ceramic cell base, into the steel housing, and from the housing into the bracket, and the heat was moving faster than the insulation could block it.

"Mission AI, is the bracket temperature rising linearly or exponentially?"

"Exponentially. The rate of increase is accelerating. At current rate, the bracket will reach two hundred fifty degrees in approximately six minutes."

Ravi looked at Arun. The young technician had gone from nervous to focused — a transformation Arun recognized because he felt it himself. Fear was a signal. Focus was the response.

"Can we add cooling to the bracket?"

"If I divert more coolant —" Arun pulled up the thermal model, ran a quick calculation. "Maybe. The primary heat exchanger has unused capacity, but it would mean routing coolant through the mounting structure instead of just the cell housing. We'd need to add a tube. We'd need to clamp it to the bracket. We'd need to —"

"Arun." Elena from the doorway. "How long?"

"Maybe two minutes of rising. Then I can try."

"Try. But prepare the shutoff. If the bracket hits two forty-five, we kill it."

Arun was already moving. He grabbed a length of the same half-inch copper tubing that the secondary heat exchanger was made from — there was spare, because Jonah had bought extra, because Jonah always bought extra — and bent it by hand into a U-shape that would fit around the brackets. His hands were steady. That was the thing about Arun under pressure: he didn't get faster or louder. He got quieter and more precise.

Ravi was at the coolant line, isolating the secondary loop from the main flow and preparing it for rerouting. "I can feed this through the copper coil."

"Do it. I'll clamp it to the bracket."

Arun pressed the copper tubing against the aluminum bracket. Even through his glove, he could feel the warmth — not the searing heat of seven hundred fifty degrees, but a solid, threatening warmth that said *this is getting too hot.* He tightened the hose clamps — two of them, one at each end — connecting the copper tube to the glycol coolant line. The tube would carry cold coolant directly against the hot bracket, stealing heat by conduction. A heat sink, improvised in ninety seconds.

"Rerouting coolant now," Ravi said, opening a valve.

The flow meter twitched, then settled at a new reading. Coolant was now flowing through the improvised bracket cooler as well as the primary heat exchanger.

Arun watched the bracket temperature. Two hundred thirty-eight. Two hundred forty. Two hundred forty-one.

Still rising.

"Rate of increase is slowing," Mission AI said. "But it is still rising. Two hundred forty-two. Two hundred forty-three."

"Come on," Arun said to the bracket. Not a prayer. A request to physics to finish the job the improvisation had started.

Two hundred forty-four. Two hundred forty-four point five. Two hundred forty-four point eight.

Steady.

"It's stabilized," Ravi said, and the relief in his voice was audible. "Two hundred forty-five. Not rising anymore."

"But it is very close to the shutoff limit," Elena said. "Arun."

"I know." Arun looked at the full thermal picture — not just the bracket, but the entire system. "Mission AI, full thermal map. Every sensor."

"Compiling. Forty-two sensors reporting."

A map appeared on Arun's tablet — a color-coded representation of the unit's temperature distribution, from cool blue at the coolant inlet to violent white at the core of the electrolysis stack. Most of the map was in the expected range. But there were hot spots — places where the temperature was higher than the model predicted, clustered around the lower half of the unit where the mounting bracket and the base insulation were located.

"The insulation at the base is insufficient," Arun said. "We put the same thickness on all sides — three layers of aerogel blanket. But the bottom of the unit is receiving heat from two sources: the cells above, and the waste heat from the resistance heater below. The insulation is saturated. It's doing its maximum, and its maximum is not enough."

"Can we add more?" Ravi asked.

"Not while it's running. The surface temperature is too high. Anyone who got close enough to add insulation would be risking a burn through the glove."

"Then what?"

Arun was looking at the numbers. The oxygen production flow meter had climbed to point zero six liters per minute — six times what it had been five minutes ago, but still well short of the target rate. The power draw was steady at ninety percent of maximum. The coolant outlet temperature was sixty-two degrees and climbing — slowly, but climbing, which meant the coolant itself was saturating, absorbing heat faster than the heat exchanger could reject it.

And the bracket — stabilized, but only barely.

"Mission AI, project the trend forward. Current rates, no change in configuration."

"Running." A pause. "At current rates, the coolant outlet will reach its maximum operating temperature of seventy-five degrees in approximately twenty-two minutes. The bracket temperature will remain near two hundred forty-five, because the improvised cooler is sufficient to hold it. But —" The AI paused. The pause meant something was about to get worse. "The core temperature will continue to climb. At ninety percent power, the core is currently at seven hundred fifty-four degrees and rising at approximately one degree per minute. At this rate, it will reach eight hundred degrees in forty-six minutes. Cell degradation will begin. Seal failure is probable within sixty to seventy minutes."

"So the system has no stable operating point," Arun said. Not a question.

"Not at current heat rejection capacity. The unit is a thermal accumulator — it absorbs more heat than it rejects. Given enough time, it will reach a temperature at which hardware fails."

Ravi looked at Arun. "So we can run it for less than an hour, and then we have to shut it down. That's not a production plant. That's a timed thermal event."

"I know."

"Mission AI, what would it take to reach stable operation?"

"Additional heat rejection capacity of approximately four kilowatts. The current system rejects six kilowatts at maximum coolant flow. Stable operation at ninety percent power requires approximately ten. The Sterling Generator waste heat exchanger is already at maximum utilization. The secondary heat exchanger is undersized for this application — the copper coil has insufficient surface area, and the module air temperature is already twenty-six degrees and rising."

The workshop was getting hotter. Arun had not noticed until Mission AI said it — twenty-six degrees was only mildly uncomfortable. But the trend was the thing. Twenty-six now. Twenty-seven in ten minutes. Twenty-eight in twenty. If the unit kept running, the workshop would become a hostile environment.

And there was something else. Arun was reading the electrical data — the current draw from the power bus. Eighteen kilowatts at ninety percent was sixteen point two. The bus was feeding it from the nuclear reactor, which had more than enough capacity. But the voltage was sagging slightly — a drop of two point one percent, small enough to ignore individually, significant when combined with the thermal trend. The voltage sag meant increased resistive losses in the power cables. More heat, generated not in the unit but in the cables leading to it. Heat that had nowhere to go.

"Arun," Elena said. Her voice had not changed — flat, calm, demanding the truth. "How bad is it?"

Arun looked at the tablet, then at the unit, then at Ravi whose hand was still resting near the manual shutoff valve, then at Elena in the doorway.

"Bad," he said. "The system is accumulating heat faster than it can shed it. The numbers say we have — forty-six minutes before the core reaches the degradation threshold. The coolant loop is approaching saturation. The workshop is warming. And the power bus is showing voltage sag from the additional load, which means more heat in the cables."

"Can it be fixed while running?"

"Maybe. But I don't know what the fix is yet. Adding more heat exchangers means shutting down and reconfiguring the plumbing. I can't do that with the unit hot. The bracket temp would spike if we lost the improvised cooler."

The alarms escalated. Not one — two. A second alarm had joined the first.

"What's the second?" Elena asked.

Mission AI answered: "The pressure relief valve inlet is reading elevated pressure. Not yet at the set point, but approaching. The backpressure in the oxygen product line is increasing — likely due to the storage vessel being warmer than expected. The heat from the unit is warming the storage vessel through the connecting pipe. Warmer gas occupies more volume at the same mass. The vessel pressure is climbing."

Ravi checked the storage vessel pressure gauge. "Eight hundred kilopascals. Rated for twelve hundred. We have four hundred kPa of margin."

"How fast is it climbing?" Arun asked.

"Approximately eight kilopascals per minute. At current rate, the vessel will reach its pressure limit in sixty-two minutes."

"Another clock," Elena said. "We have two clocks. Forty-six minutes for the cells. Sixty-two minutes for the vessel. The shorter one wins."

Ravi was standing at the manual valve now, his hand on the wheel, his eyes on the temperature display. He was doing exactly what Elena had asked: watching the number that mattered, ready to act.

"Arun," Ravi said. "I need to know what number I'm watching for. Seven hundred seventy was the shutoff. But the system is still below that."

"Seven hundred seventy," Arun confirmed. "But the number might change. If the bracket temperature starts rising again, or the coolant outlet passes seventy, or the storage vessel exceeds eleven hundred kPa — any of those, we shut down."

"Understood."

The workshop was now twenty-seven degrees. The air was still, thick with the smell of hot metal and the faint ozone crackle of high-current electrical systems. Somewhere in the background, the module's environmental control system was working harder than normal, the compressor cycling more frequently to try to maintain setpoint against the additional heat load.

Jonah had appeared in the doorway, drawn by the alarms. He took in the scene — the unit, the tablet, the copper pipe improvisation, the sweat on Ravi's face — with the quick assessment of someone who had built the thing and now had to watch it threaten to destroy itself.

"What's wrong?" Jonah asked.

"Heat. We're generating more than we can reject. The unit will cook itself if we let it run."

"Can we blow more air on it?"

"The secondary heat exchanger is already —" Arun stopped. "Actually. Can we?"

"The module air is at twenty-seven degrees. If we blow ambient through the unit at higher velocity, the convective heat transfer from the housing will increase. It's not much, but —"

"But it's something. How much?" Arun pulled up a convection model on his tablet, ran a fast calculation. "Increasing air velocity past the housing from zero to two meters per second would add approximately point eight kilowatts of heat rejection. Not enough on its own. But combined with the bracket cooler, it might flatten the curve."

"I can rig a fan," Jonah said. "We've got that twelve-inch blower from the air filtration unit. I can mount it on a stand, aim it at the base of the unit, and push air upward through the clearance gap between the housing and the pallet. It'll flow over the insulation blankets, pick up waste heat, and dump it into the upper volume of the workshop. The temperature will climb faster in the room, but the unit will run cooler."

"Do it," Elena said. No hesitation. A small improvement was better than no improvement, and on Mars, small improvements added up to survival.

Jonah was already moving. He had the fan on its stand and aimed at the base of the unit within two minutes. It was a twelve-inch axial blower — the kind used to circulate air through dust filters — and it moved air in the blunt, uncontrolled way of industrial ventilation: not elegant, not precise, but effective. He plugged it into a nearby outlet, flipped the switch, and the room filled with the industrial hum of forced air.

Arun watched the thermal map. The housing temperature — which had been creeping upward — slowed, then stopped, then began a very slow decline. Point eight kilowatts. Not enough to solve the problem. But enough to slow it.

"Mission AI," Arun said. "Re-run the time-to-failure projection with the additional convective cooling."

"Running." Three seconds. "Core temperature will reach eight hundred degrees in approximately fifty-eight minutes, up from forty-six. Twelve minutes gained. The coolant outlet will still reach seventy-five degrees in approximately nineteen minutes. The bracket temperature remains stable at two hundred forty-five degrees. The storage vessel pressure will reach eleven hundred kPa in approximately sixty-seven minutes."

Twelve minutes. The margin had grown from forty-six to fifty-eight. But fifty-eight minutes was still a timer, not a stable operating point.

Ravi was watching his display. "Flow rate is climbing. Point zero eight liters per minute. We're making oxygen."

"We're also making a problem," Arun said.

## Scene 3

The alarms tripled.

Not three separate alarm tones — the same alarm, multiplied, from three different sensors all exceeding their thresholds within the same ten seconds. Mission AI consolidated the report in a single breath:

"Coolant outlet temperature: seventy-two degrees, approaching seventy-five limit. Storage vessel pressure: nine hundred thirty kPa, climbing at eleven kPa per minute. Core temperature: seven hundred sixty-two degrees, rising at zero point eight degrees per minute. Three systems approaching limits simultaneously."

Arun stared at the tablet. Three clocks, all ticking. The coolant was the most urgent — once the coolant exceeded seventy-five degrees, the glycol-water mixture would begin to degrade, losing its heat transfer efficiency and potentially causing vapor lock in the lines. If the coolant stopped flowing, the entire thermal management system would collapse, and the unit would cook in seconds.

"Shed the secondary load," Arun said. "Ravi, close the bypass valve that's feeding the bracket cooler back into the main loop. Divert all coolant through the primary heat exchanger only."

"But the bracket —"

"The bracket has enough thermal mass to withstand a brief temperature spike. If the coolant line goes vapor lock, we lose everything anyway. Divert to primary only."

Ravi turned the valve. The flow meter dropped — the total flow was lower now, concentrated in one line. The coolant outlet temperature dropped from seventy-two to seventy, then sixty-nine. A small gain, but the trend had reversed.

The bracket temperature spiked. Two hundred forty-five to two hundred fifty to two hundred fifty-five — then it slowed, held, and began a very gradual climb. Two hundred fifty-seven. Fifty-eight. Fifty-nine.

"Bracket at two hundred fifty-nine and still climbing," Mission AI said. The voice was steady, clinical. "The aluminum alloy will not fail at this temperature for several more minutes. But the margin is narrowing."

"Core?"

"Seven hundred sixty-five degrees. Still rising. The additional convective cooling has flattened the curve but not reversed it."

Arun stepped closer to the unit, close enough to hear the deep, resonant hum of the electrolysis current passing through the ceramic cells. It was a sound he had only heard in simulations — a low, steady vibration at sixty hertz, the frequency of the AC power converted to DC for the electrolysis reaction. The sound of splitting carbon dioxide. The sound of making air.

He looked at the unit the way he would look at a patient — not at the display, not at the sensors, but at the physical thing itself. The stainless steel housing was discoloring — a dark brown patina forming on the hottest surfaces, the color of metal that had been held at temperature for too long. The insulation blankets were intact but the outermost layer was slightly discolored, showing the thermal gradient that the design had not anticipated. The copper pipe improvisation for the bracket cooler was working — he could see condensation forming on the outer surface of the tube, a visible sign of the temperature differential between the coolant inside and the hot bracket outside.

And the fan — Jonah's twelve-inch blower — was pushing air upward past the housing at a velocity that rattled the loose edge of an insulation blanket.

"Arun." Elena's voice. Calm, but with an edge. "Ravi's looking at the storage vessel gauge. Ten hundred kPa. Climbing."

"I see it."

"We need answers, not monitoring."

Arun took a breath. He closed his eyes for one second — a deliberate pause, not a moment of panic, but a moment of synthesis — and then he opened them and spoke.

"Many machines fail the same way people do — they get overwhelmed faster than they can shed what is hurting them. This unit is running too hot because we asked it to do more than its thermal design allows. That's not a flaw in the machine. It's a flaw in our understanding of the machine. We built it from parts that were each designed for a different job, and we assumed that the combined thermal behavior would be the sum of the individual parts. But it isn't. Thermal systems don't add. They multiply. Each hot spot makes the next hot spot hotter, and the next, and the next, until the curve goes vertical."

He was talking loudly enough for Ravi to hear, but he was also talking for himself — articulating the problem as a way of thinking through the solution.

"The unit generates eighteen kilowatts of heat at full power. Six go into making oxygen — that's the electrochemical energy stored in the O₂-CO bond that we broke. Twelve kilowatts are pure waste heat that has nowhere to go. The primary heat exchanger can handle four. The secondary was built to handle one point two. The convective cooling from the fan added point eight. That's six. We're short — six kilowatts short."

"Can we reduce the input power?" Elena asked.

"Reduce power, reduce oxygen. We'd be running a very expensive heater. The whole point was oxygen production."

"Can we increase cooling?"

"Not with what we have in the workshop right now. The primary heat exchanger is at maximum flow. The secondary is —" He stopped. The secondary was the copper coil and radiator panel. The radiator panel was dumping heat into module air. The module air was at twenty-eight degrees and rising. What if the radiator wasn't dumping heat into air? What if it was dumping heat into something colder?

"Mission AI," Arun said. "What's the heat rejection capacity of the exterior hull? If we routed the secondary coolant through a pipe that passed through the module wall and radiated directly to the Martian ambient —"

"The ambient temperature is minus sixty degrees Celsius. The radiative and conductive heat transfer to the exterior would be —" A pause. "Significant. Approximately eight kilowatts, assuming sufficient pipe length and cross-sectional area. However, penetrating the module wall carries pressure integrity risk. Any penetration must be sealed to maintain hull integrity."

"I can seal a penetration," Jonah said from the doorway. He had been listening. "Bulkhead fitting, double O-ring, rated for full module pressure. We have spares."

"Jonah," Elena said. "How long to install?"

"Five minutes, if the pipe is prepped. Ten if it isn't."

"Make it five."

Jonah was already moving. He returned three minutes later with a bulkhead fitting — a heavy brass connector designed to pass a pipe through a pressure wall while maintaining seal integrity — and a length of half-inch copper tubing. He knelt at the module wall near the workshop's exterior bulkhead, measured, cut a hole with the rotary tool — sparks showered the floor grating — and threaded the fitting through the wall.

The workshop depressurized slightly during the process — the ambient pressure dropped by two hundredths of a percent, a blip that Mission AI caught and reported and then dismissed as insignificant. Jonah tightened the fitting, checked the seal with a pressure decay test, and nodded at Ravi.

"Ready to connect," Jonah said.

"Ravi, isolate the secondary loop from the module-air heat exchanger. Reconnect to Jonah's new pipe. We'll dump waste heat directly to Mars."

Ravi worked the valve sequence with the competence of someone who had done this kind of plumbing work dozens of times — isolate, drain, connect, repressurize, bleed air. The glycol coolant loop was a closed system, and opening it carried the risk of introducing air bubbles, which would reduce heat transfer and potentially cause localized overheating. Ravi bled the line carefully, watching the sight glass until only liquid was visible.

"Secondary loop reconnected. Flow resuming."

Arun watched the coolant temperature. The new heat exchanger — a copper pipe now passing through the module wall into minus-sixty-degree Martian air — would have dramatically more cooling capacity than the radiator panel. The temperature differential had gone from approximately fifty degrees (62°C coolant to 12°C module air, after warming above) to approximately 120 degrees (62°C coolant to minus 60°C ambient). Heat transfer proportional to temperature difference. The math favored them massively.

The coolant outlet temperature dropped from sixty-nine to sixty-four in ten seconds.

Fifty-eight in the next ten.

Fifty-two.

"Forty-seven," Mission AI said. "The exterior heat exchanger is performing at approximately seven point six kilowatts rejection. The primary heat exchanger continues at four point eight. Total system rejection: twelve point four kilowatts."

Twelve point four out. The unit was generating twelve kilowatts of waste heat. They were now rejecting more than they were generating.

"Core temperature," Arun said.

"Seven hundred sixty-seven degrees — still rising, but the rate has dropped from zero point eight to zero point three degrees per minute. The temperature curve is flattening. The system is approaching equilibrium."

Arun let himself breathe. The curve was flattening. That was the thing that mattered — not the absolute temperature, but the derivative. A rising temperature that was rising more slowly was a system approaching stability. The derivative heading toward zero meant equilibrium was coming.

But the system wasn't there yet. And the derivative was still positive.

"Storage vessel?" Arun asked.

"Seven hundred eighty kPa," Ravi said. "Slower climb. Three kPa per minute now, down from eleven. The vessel is still warming from the incoming oxygen, but the rate has dropped."

"Good. We're close to stable. Let it run. Nobody touch anything for five minutes."

Five minutes. The longest five minutes of Arun's career, and it was only the first five minutes of what would be — if this worked — years of continuous operation.

The numbers drifted, inching toward stability like a boat finding its mooring in a crosswind. Core temperature: seven hundred sixty-eight, seven hundred sixty-nine, seven hundred sixty-nine point five. Slower. Slower. The climb was barely measurable now.

Fan noise. The hum of electrical current. The deep, steady vibration of the electrolysis stack splitting carbon dioxide molecule by molecule. The smell of hot metal and ozone and the faint chemical tang of glycol. A workshop on Mars, running a machine that made air, and the air was building in a storage vessel and the machine was not destroying itself.

"Mission AI," Arun said quietly. "Core temperature derivative."

"Zero point zero two degrees per minute. Effectively stable. The system has reached thermal equilibrium at approximately seven hundred seventy degrees Celsius."

"Seven hundred," Ravi said, reading the flow meter. "Flow rate is point one two liters per minute. Oxygen purity: ninety-four percent."

A point one two liters per minute. That wasn't a start anymore. That was a production rate. That was enough oxygen, over the course of a day, to measurably extend the colony's reserve. Over the course of a week, it would add days of breathing room. Over the course of a month, it would change the oxygen budget from precarious to adequate.

But the unit was at seven hundred seventy degrees Celsius — two degrees above the target operating temperature, seven degrees above the ideal. The seals were operating above their design limit. The cells were running hot. The bracket was at two hundred sixty-four degrees Celsius, still holding but close to the shutoff threshold.

It was running. But it wasn't clean. It wasn't elegant. It was a system pushed to its limit, held in equilibrium by a series of improvisations, one of which involved a copper pipe running through the module wall to the Martian wilderness because the workshop was too warm to dump heat into the room.

It would work. But it would not work forever.

---

## Scene 4

The storage vessel pressure alarm sounded at 842 kilopascals — still well below the 1,200-set limit, but climbing at a rate that suggested something else was wrong.

"Mission AI, vessel pressure trend. Why is it still climbing when the oxygen flow rate is stable?"

"The vessel temperature is rising. The connecting pipe between the electrolysis unit and the storage vessel is conducting heat from the unit to the vessel. The vessel was designed to store oxygen at ambient temperature. It is currently at thirty-four degrees and rising. As the temperature rises, the gas pressure increases — ideal gas law. Volume is constant, mass is increasing from the oxygen flow, and temperature is increasing from the conducted heat. Both mass and temperature are driving the pressure up."

Arun looked at the connecting pipe. It was stainless steel tubing — rigid, insulated, but insufficiently insulated for a line carrying gas from a seven-hundred-seventy-degree source. The insulation was doing its job partially, but partially was not enough. Some of that heat was making its way through the insulation and along the pipe, raising the temperature of the vessel at the far end.

"We need to break the thermal coupling between the unit and the vessel," Arun said. "The pipe is conducting heat directly from the stack to the tank."

"Can we add insulation?" Ravi asked. "More layers?"

"Maybe. But the pipe surface is at — " Arun checked the thermal map. "One hundred eighty degrees. Too hot to add insulation. We'd burn the person installing it, and the insulation material wouldn't survive the surface temperature long enough to be effective."

Jonah knelt beside the pipe, his hand hovering a few centimeters from the insulation surface. "There's a way," he said. "A thermal break. If we cut the pipe mid-span and insert a section of material with low thermal conductivity — PTFE, ceramic, something that doesn't conduct heat — we break the conduction path. The gas still flows, but the heat doesn't."

"PTFE melts at two hundred sixty degrees," Arun said. "The gas coming through is at — Mission AI, gas temperature at the pipe outlet from the unit."

"The oxygen product gas exits the electrolysis stack at approximately one hundred twenty degrees Celsius. It cools as it flows through the insulated pipe — the insulation is effective at reducing conductive heat loss, which ironically means the gas itself stays hot longer."

"So the gas in the pipe is one hundred twenty degrees, cooling slowly. A PTFE break in the middle of the pipe would survive — one hundred twenty is well below two hundred sixty. But we'd need to cut the pipe, insert the break, and reconnect while the system is running. That means —"

"That means venting a small amount of oxygen while I do the cut," Jonah said. "Thirty seconds of vent. Acceptable loss for what we gain."

"Do it," Arun said.

Jonah pulled a section of PTFE pipe from his material stock — white, opaque, thermally insulating, rated for temperatures up to two hundred sixty degrees. He cut it to the required length — approximately six centimeters — and slid it onto one end of the steel pipe. Then, with the system running and oxygen flowing and the alarms still chirping in the background at a lower frequency, he used a tube cutter to sever the stainless steel pipe at its midpoint.

A puff of warm, oxygen-rich gas escaped the cut. Ravi flinched — oxygen-enriched atmospheres made everything flammable, and a stray spark in the workshop could have ignited — but Jonah held the two pipe ends apart, purged the gap with inert nitrogen from his tool kit, and then brought them back together with the PTFE section between them.

The PTFE created a six-centimeter gap between the hot pipe section near the unit and the cooler pipe section near the vessel. Heat would not bridge that gap. The gas would flow — gas molecules are small, and they would pass through the six-centimeter gap easily — but thermal energy would not conduct through a material that was, by design, a poor conductor.

Jonah clamped the connections with stainless steel hose clamps, verified the seal with a leak check, and stepped back.

Arun watched the vessel temperature. Thirty-five degrees. Thirty-five point two. Thirty-five point three.

Steady. No longer rising.

"Gas temperature at the vessel inlet?" Arun asked.

"Forty-two degrees Celsius," Mission AI said. "Down from seventy-eight. The thermal break is effective. The gas is cooling through the PTFE section. Heat is not being conducted along the pipe."

Ravi read the vessel pressure gauge. "Eight hundred forty-five kPa. Stable. No longer climbing."

"Flow rate?"

"Point one two liters per minute. Unchanged by the thermal break. Oxygen production is unaffected."

Arun exhaled. Four separate thermal problems — the bracket, the coolant, the core, and the vessel — and all four had been addressed, not by design, but by intervention. Each one had been a small thing. A copper pipe. A fan. A bulkhead fitting. A six-centimeter piece of plastic. But each one had been a small thing at the right place at the right time, and that was the difference between a system that worked and a system that cooked itself.

"Mission AI — full system status. Are we stable?"

"Running the full diagnostic." A pause of four seconds — Mission AI was checking every sensor, every trend, every derivative, not just the current values but the rates of change and the rates of change of the rates of change. "Core temperature: seven hundred seventy degrees Celsius, stable, derivative within point zero one degrees per minute. Coolant outlet: forty-six degrees Celsius, stable. Bracket temperature: two hundred sixty-three degrees, stable and slowly declining. Storage vessel: eight hundred forty-five kPa, stable, temperature thirty-four degrees and slowly declining. Oxygen flow: point one two liters per minute. Oxygen purity: ninety-four percent. All forty-two sensors reporting. All parameters within operational limits. The system is stable."

Arun looked at the tablet. The thermal map was a different picture than it had been twenty minutes ago. The hot spots had cooled. The gradient was gentler. The unit was no longer a collection of near-failures held together by improvisation. It was — it was not elegant. It would never be elegant. But it was operating. It was producing oxygen at a rate that exceeded the original MOXIE unit by a factor of approximately twelve. And it was doing so without destroying itself.

He looked at Ravi. The young technician was still standing at the manual valve, but his hand was no longer hovering. It was resting on the wheel, relaxed.

"We're good," Arun said.

Ravi nodded. His expression was the expression of someone who had been expecting something to go wrong and had been proven wrong, and who was experiencing the particular quiet satisfaction of having done his job correctly under pressure.

"Elena," Arun said, looking at the doorway.

Elena was still there. She had not moved. Her arms were crossed again, not in defensiveness now, but in the posture of assessment. She had watched the whole thing — the alarms, the improvisations, the near-misses, the recovery. She had trusted her engineer to fix the problem, and her technician to shut it down if the engineer failed, and both of them had done their jobs.

"You fixed it," she said.

"We managed it," Arun corrected. "There's a difference. We didn't fix the underlying problem — the thermal design is inadequate for full power. What we did was add enough cooling to find a stable operating point. The unit will run. It will produce oxygen. But it needs a permanent thermal redesign before we rely on it for long-term production."

"How long can it run as-is?"

"Indefinitely, as long as the improvised cooling stays in place. The fan, the exterior heat exchanger, the bracket cooler, the thermal break on the product line — all four need to remain operational. If any one of them fails, we need to shut down within — I'd estimate five to ten minutes, depending on which one."

"Five to ten minutes," Ravi repeated. "Which means someone needs to be monitoring it constantly."

"Or the AI does," Arun said. "Mission AI, can you monitor the four critical parameters and alert us in real time if any deviates beyond acceptable range?"

"I am already monitoring all forty-two parameters at one-second intervals. I can alert you within three seconds of any deviation. I can also — if you authorize me — automatically engage a controlled power reduction if the core temperature exceeds seven hundred eighty degrees. I would reduce power by twenty percent, which would reduce heat generation proportionally. You would lose oxygen production temporarily, but you would avoid thermal damage."

Arun considered this. Giving the AI autonomous control over the power to the oxygen unit was a significant decision. It meant the AI could reduce production without human authorization — a trade-off between safety and output. On one hand, the AI was faster than any human at detecting and responding to thermal anomalies. On the other hand, reducing oxygen production without authorization could create problems if the colony was depending on that oxygen for a critical operation.

"Authorized," Arun said. "Automatic power reduction at seven hundred eighty. Alert me immediately when you do it."

"Understood. I have the control protocol loaded. I will respond within three seconds."

Elena nodded. "Good. I want Mission AI watching this unit the way a nurse watches an ICU patient. Not because it will fail — because we can't afford for it to fail."

"Agreed," Arun said. "Now — can we increase power? If the system is stable at ninety percent, can we go to ninety-five? The oxygen flow would increase proportionally."

Ravi was already looking at the thermal map. "At ninety-five, the heat input increases by about nine hundred watts. Our cooling margin is —" He looked at Mission AI.

"Current cooling surplus is zero point four kilowatts — the system is rejecting twelve point four kilowatts at an input of twelve kilowatts waste heat. A nine-hundred-watt increase would push the system back into negative balance. It would begin climbing again, slowly, but climbing. I estimate you could sustain ninety-five percent power for approximately two hours before reaching the core temperature limit."

"Two hours of higher production, then we have to drop back."

"Or increase cooling further," Jonah said. "I could add a second exterior pipe. Double the heat rejection to the exterior."

"Can the bulkhead handle two penetrations?" Elena asked.

"Two bulkhead fittings, spaced apart — yes. The wall has the structural capacity. I'd need approximately forty minutes to install."

"Forty minutes of lost production while you drill a second hole through the module wall," Arun said. "During which the unit continues running at ninety percent, producing oxygen but not as much as it could."

He looked at the flow meter. Point one two liters per minute. Over an hour, that was approximately seven point two liters of oxygen. Over a day — if the unit ran continuously — approximately one hundred seventy-three liters. The colony consumed approximately nine hundred liters of oxygen per day at current rates. The original MOXIE unit provided approximately three hundred liters per day. The new unit, even at ninety percent, would add one hundred forty-three liters per day on top of the existing production.

It wasn't a revolution. It was a margin. And margins were what kept colonies alive.

"Leave it at ninety," Arun said. "Don't push toward ninety-five until we have the second heat exchanger installed. We have time. The unit is stable. I don't want to trade stability for production and then have to rebuild the whole thing from scratch."

Ravi nodded, relieved. "Ninety percent. Locked in."

---

## Scene 5

The workshop settled into a new rhythm.

The fan continued its steady hum. The electrolysis stack continued its deep, sixty-hertz vibration. The oxygen flowed — point one two liters per minute — into the storage vessel, where the pressure gauge held steady at eight hundred forty-five kilopascals and the temperature had begun a slow, steady decline from thirty-four back toward ambient.

Arun sat on a stool near the unit, his tablet on his knee, watching the numbers. Not because he mistrusted Mission AI — he trusted the AI completely, more than he trusted most humans, which was a statement that had taken him years to arrive at and that he would not have voiced aloud in the early days of the mission. But because watching was what engineers did. Watching was the act of paying attention to the physical world, of maintaining the relationship between intention and reality, of verifying that the numbers on the screen meant what they said they meant.

Ravi had moved to a workbench and was making notes — actual pen-on-paper notes, the kind that survived power failures. "I'll document everything," he said. "Every alarm, every intervention, every temperature reading. If this unit ever behaves differently, we need to know what worked the first time."

"Good," Arun said. "Include the fan. Include the copper pipe. Include the PTFE break. We don't want the next person to think the unit was designed this way. It wasn't. It was held together by hope and half-inch tubing."

Ravi smiled. The kind of smile that comes after a near-miss, when the adrenaline has faded and the reality of what almost happened is beginning to sink in.

Elena stepped into the workshop, her footsteps quieter now that the alarms had stopped. She carried a tablet of her own — the base status report, the one she reviewed every six hours, updated with the oxygen production data that had just become relevant.

"Oxygen reserves," she said, sitting on the stool next to Arun. "Before the expanded unit came online, Mission AI projected that our current reserves — including the original MOXIE production — would last approximately fourteen months. With this unit running at its current rate, how does that change?"

Arun pulled up the projection. "At point one two liters per minute continuous production, the expanded unit adds approximately one hundred seventy-three liters per day. Added to the original MOXIE's three hundred liters per day, total oxygen production becomes four hundred seventy-three liters per day. Current consumption is approximately nine hundred liters per day. We're still below consumption, but we've closed half the gap."

"Half the gap is still a gap."

"It's a narrowing gap. Four hundred seventy-three liters in — nine hundred out — means we're losing four hundred twenty-seven liters per day. Without the expanded unit, we were losing six hundred liters per day. We've extended the reserve lifetime from fourteen months to approximately twenty-one months."

"Seven months gained from a machine that almost destroyed itself," Elena said.

"Seven months. And if we install the second heat exchanger, push the unit to ninety-five percent, and keep it stable — we might reach twenty-four months. That puts us at the threshold where local oxygen production can match consumption. At that point, the reserves stop declining and become a buffer instead of a countdown."

Elena absorbed this. Seven months was not infinity. It was not safety. It was breathing room — literal and figurative — and on Mars, breathing room was the difference between a colony that was surviving and a colony that was planning.

"Can we scale it further?" Elena asked. "A third unit. Or a second electrolysis stack in the same housing."

"Maybe. But each unit brings its own thermal challenges. And our power budget is finite. The reactor can handle it — the reactor has headroom. But every kilowatt we put into oxygen production is a kilowatt we're not putting into something else. Water extraction. Greenhouse lighting. Life support. Communications."

"I know." Elena looked at the unit. "But seven months changes what we can plan for. A seven-month extension means we can take risks we couldn't take before. We can send a crew further from base. We can expand the greenhouse. We can do EVA work without checking the oxygen gauge after every sortie."

"That's the point," Arun said. "This isn't about the number. It's about the freedom the number creates. When you know you have air, you stop thinking about air, and you start thinking about what you can do with the time the air buys you."

Elena nodded. She was already doing it — he could see the shift in her thinking, the way the oxygen production had gone from an engineering problem to a strategic resource in the span of a single successful run. She was recalculating. She was always recalculating.

Behind them, the workshop hummed. The fan turned. The electrolysis stack split carbon dioxide. The oxygen flowed into the vessel and the pressure held and the numbers on Arun's tablet were green — not perfectly green, not the green of a system that had been designed right the first time, but the green of a system that had been pushed to the edge, almost failed, and been pulled back by human hands and human attention and an AI that had monitored every parameter with the patient, unblinking vigilance of a mind that never slept.

Ravi finished his notes and closed his notebook. "I'll take the next monitoring shift," he said. "Four hours. Go eat something, Arun. You've been in this workshop since before the power-up."

"I'm fine."

"You look like you've been run through the Sterling generator. Go eat."

Arun stood. His legs felt stiff — sitting for three hours watching numbers does that — and his shirt was damp with sweat from the warm workshop air. He looked at the unit one more time before leaving. It looked the way it had always looked: a vertical assembly of stainless steel and ceramic on a reinforced pallet, with a fan pointed at its base and a copper pipe running through the wall to the cold outside. Nothing about its appearance had changed. Everything about its significance had.

It was running. It was making oxygen. It had not destroyed itself.

Those were the three things that mattered.

Arun walked toward the doorway. Elena was standing, her tablet under her arm, already moving toward the comm station to update the mission log. Ravi was settling into the monitor's stool, his eyes on the tablet, his hand resting lightly on the manual shutoff valve. Mission AI was watching — always watching — forty-two sensors sampled once per second, every parameter tracked, every derivative calculated, every trend projected forward into a future that was no longer quite so dark.

The workshop, for the first time in three weeks of construction and stress and near-disaster, was a place where something worked.

## Scene 1

The workshop smelled of cutting fluid and ozone — metal being pushed to its limits, welds still cooling, capacitors that had been charged one too many times.

The oxygen plant sat in the center of the machine bay like a mechanical patient waiting for surgery. A vertical assembly of stainless steel and ceramic, two meters tall, bolted to a reinforced pallet with six M12 anchors. Not pretty. Nothing built on Mars from salvaged parts was pretty. The two hundred fourteenth was the one that had kept him up: the thermal mass calculation. The actual heat capacity of ceramic cells manufactured for a different application and repurposed. The conductivity of welds Jonah had made at three in the morning under halogen work lights. The efficiency of an improvised heat exchanger built from greenhouse irrigation pipe. The thermal resistance of insulation blankets layered in an arrangement determined by what was available, not by design.

"Mission AI, run the thermal model. Conservative estimates — upper bound on heat generation, lower bound on heat rejection."

Heat generation will then exceed rejection capacity by approximately twenty-one percent. Temperature will continue to climb. At eight hundred degrees, the ceramic cell separators begin to degrade. At eight hundred fifty, the seals fail. At nine hundred, the stainless steel housing softens."

"How long to eight hundred?"

"Nineteen minutes from ignition, assuming no intervention."

Arun closed his eyes briefly. "And if we shut down at seven hundred seventy?"

"Residual heat will drive the temperature up another forty to sixty degrees. You would likely reach eight hundred ten to eight hundred thirty. Above the degradation threshold."

"Uncomfortable for the hardware," Arun said.

"Not for the crew."

"If the seals don't hold?" she asked.

"Can you close the valve from here?"

"Core temperature at one hundred eighty degrees, rising linearly. Gradient within tolerance."

"Forty percent. Three hundred twenty. Good rate."

"Good. Resuming ramp."

"Electrolysis won't start until seven hundred fifty," Arun said. "But we might see early ion conduction."

Ravi's hand was on the dial. "One hundred percent in three — two — one."

"It's a start."

Martian CO₂, split at seven hundred fifty degrees into oxygen and carbon monoxide by zirconia conducting oxide ions through its crystal lattice. The same chemistry NASA's MOXIE had demonstrated on Perseverance, scaled up twelve times, built in a workshop on a planet that had never had a single breath of oxygen.

"Flow climbing. Point zero two. Point zero three. Purity at ninety-two percent. Enough for storage."
