"Mission AI, coolant loop temperature."

## Scene 2

Six minutes in, the alarms started.

Not caution tones — the sharp, urgent warble that meant limits were being exceeded.

"Temperature at the lower cell mounting bracket has reached two hundred eighty degrees," Mission AI said, and there was a new quality to the voice — not panic, but the particular intensity of an AI whose models had been surprised. "Projected maximum was two hundred thirty. The bracket is aluminum. Structural integrity degrades above two hundred fifty. Thirty degrees of margin."

Arun's eyes went to the thermal map. The aluminum angle iron that Jonah had bolted to support the stack's weight was hotter than predicted. The insulation blankets hadn't been enough. Heat was conducting through the cell base, into the housing, into the bracket, faster than the insulation could block.

"Is the bracket temperature rising linearly or exponentially?"

"Exponentially. Rate of increase is accelerating. In approximately six minutes, the bracket will reach two hundred fifty."

Ravi looked at Arun. Fear was a signal. Focus was the response.

"Can we cool the bracket?"

"If I divert more coolant —" Arun ran a calculation. "Maybe. Primary heat exchanger has unused capacity. Route coolant through the mounting structure. Add a tube, clamp it to the bracket."

"Arun." Elena from the doorway. "How long?"

"Two minutes to try."

"If the bracket hits two forty-five, kill it."

Ravi was at the coolant line. "I can feed this through the copper coil."

"Do it."

"Mission AI — heat rejection capacity if we routed the secondary coolant through a pipe penetrating the module wall, radiating directly to Martian ambient?"

"Ambient temperature is minus sixty degrees Celsius. Radiative and conductive transfer would be approximately eight kilowatts. However, penetrating the module wall carries pressure integrity risk."

"I can seal a penetration," Jonah said. "Bulkhead fitting, double O-ring. Spares in stock."

"Time?"

"Five minutes if the pipe is prepped. Ten if it isn't."

"Make it five."

Jonah tightened, checked the seal with a pressure decay test, nodded.

"Ravi — isolate the secondary from the module-air heat exchanger. Reconnect to the exterior pipe. Dump waste heat to Mars."

The temperature differential had gone from roughly fifty degrees to a hundred and twenty. Physics multiplied by the difference.

Coolant outlet: sixty-nine to sixty-four in ten seconds. Fifty-eight in the next. Fifty-two.

"Forty-seven," Mission AI said. "Exterior heat exchanger at seven point six kilowatts rejection. Primary at four point eight. Total: twelve point four."

Twelve point four out. Twelve in.

"Core temperature?"

"Seven hundred sixty-seven degrees — still rising, but the rate dropped from zero point eight to zero point three per minute. The curve is flattening. Approaching equilibrium."

"Vessel?"

"Seven hundred eighty kPa. Slower climb. Three per minute now."

Five minutes. The longest of Arun's career.

Numbers drifted toward stability. Seven hundred sixty-eight. Six hundred sixty-nine. Six hundred sixty-nine point five. The climb barely measurable now.

Fan noise. Electrical hum. Deep sixty-hertz vibration of the stack splitting CO₂ molecule by molecule. A workshop on Mars running a machine that made air, and the machine wasn't destroying itself.

"Mission AI — core temperature derivative."

"Zero point zero two degrees per minute. Effectively stable. Thermal equilibrium reached at approximately seven hundred seventy degrees Celsius."

"Flow rate?"

"Point one two liters per minute. Purity: ninety-four percent."

Running at seven hundred seventy — seven degrees above ideal. The seals operating above design limit. The bracket at two sixty-four, close to shutoff.

But running. Not clean. Not elegant. Held in equilibrium by a fan, a copper pipe, a bulkhead fitting, and human attention. Working because people paid attention when it mattered.

---

"Pressure alert," Mission AI said. "Vessel pressure holding at eight hundred forty-two kPa, but slowly climbing. Cause: the connecting pipe conducts heat from the unit to the storage vessel. Gas exits the stack at one hundred twenty degrees and remains hot through the insulated line. The vessel was designed for ambient-temperature storage. "Add insulation?"

"Pipe surface is at one hundred eighty. Too hot to handle. But—" Jonah was already thinking. "Thermal break. Cut the pipe mid-span. Insert PTFE — low thermal conductivity, rated to two sixty. Gas flows. Heat doesn't."

"Thirty seconds of vent," Jonah said. "Acceptable."

Gas flowing. Heat not conducting.

Vessel inlet temperature: seventy-eight down to forty-two.

"Thermal break effective. Vessel pressure: eight hundred forty-five. Stable."

"Flow?"

"Point one two. Unchanged."

Four thermal problems. Four interventions. A copper pipe, a fan, a bulkhead fitting, six centimeters of plastic — small things at the right place at the right time, the difference between a system that worked and one that cooked itself.

"We're good," Arun said.

Ravi's hand was no longer hovering over the valve. Resting on it now, relaxed.

Elena stepped forward. "You fixed it."

"We managed it. Didn't fix the thermal design — added enough cooling to find a stable point. Long-term, it needs a redesign. Right now: indefinite operation, as long as all four improvised cooling pieces stay functional. One fails, shut down within five to ten minutes."

"Then someone watches it," Elena said.

"Or the AI does. Mission AI — can you monitor the four critical parameters, alert within three seconds of deviation?"

"Authorized. Reduce at seven hundred eighty. Alert me immediately."

"Understood. Protocol loaded."

Elena nodded. "Good. I want it watched like an ICU patient. Not because it will fail. Because we can't afford it to."

"Can we increase power? Ninety-five percent?"

"Current cooling surplus: four hundred watts. A nine-hundred-watt increase pushes us back into negative balance. You'd have about two hours before exceeding core limit."

"Leave it at ninety. Point one two liters per minute. One hundred seventy-three liters per day. Added to MOXIE's three hundred — four seventy-three total. Consumption is nine hundred. Half the gap closed."

"Seven months added to reserve lifetime," Elena said.

Seven months. Not infinity. Not safety. A margin — and on Mars, margins were what separated surviving from planning.

The workshop settled into a new rhythm. Fan humming. Stack vibrating. Oxygen flowing.

Arun sat on a stool, tablet on his knee, watching the numbers. Not because he didn't trust the AI — he trusted it more than most humans — but because watching was what engineers did. Watching was the relationship between intention and reality.

Running. Making oxygen. Not destroying itself.

Three things that mattered.

"Seven months," Elena said behind him. Thinking already — recalculating, as she always did. "Seven months of breathing room changes the EVA schedule. Changes the greenhouse expansion. Changes—"

"I know."

She was already moving toward the comm station, already turning oxygen into strategy. That was a commander. That was good.

Behind them, the workshop worked. The oxygen built up in the vessel. Forty-two sensors sampled once per second. The AI watched every derivative, every trend, every rate of change of rate of change — the patient unblinking vigilance of a mind that never slept.

The machine had almost killed itself. They had pulled it back. Now it was giving them time.
